title: AI + Ethics Curricula for Middle School Youth: Lessons Learned from Three Project-Based Curricula
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper does not match the requested 2025 secondary-writing study. Instead, it reports an empirical mixed-methods evaluation of three AI literacy curricula for middle school students: Creative AI, Dancing with AI, and How to Train Your Robot. The core problem addressed is how to design accessible K-12 AI curricula that help young learners understand AI concepts, create with AI, and critically examine ethical and societal implications of AI systems. The authors frame the work around three design principles: active learning, embedded ethics, and low barriers to access.

The intervention consisted of three synchronous online, project-based summer workshops adapted from in-person formats during COVID-19. Creative AI taught generative AI and GANs through media creation and deepfake-related activities; Dancing with AI used AI-powered block-based tools and movement-based programming; and How to Train Your Robot taught machine learning and autonomous robotics using block programming and low-cost Bluetooth robots. The study used a mixed-methods approach including pre-questionnaires, workshop-specific assessments, thematic coding of student responses, and rubrics or observations of final projects.

Participants were 78 middle school students from 10 schools across 8 U.S. states, recruited through 11 in-service middle school teachers, many from Title I schools. Workshops ran online over one week, with daily sessions of 2 to 2.5 hours. Teachers were trained before and during implementation and served as co-instructors, recruiters, and teaching assistants. The context was explicitly designed to broaden participation and reduce barriers related to technical prerequisites, hardware, and student engagement in remote learning.

The main conclusions are that middle school students were already aware of AI in everyday life but often had incomplete or overly broad conceptions of what counts as AI. Across the workshops, students demonstrated growth in understanding AI concepts, engaged meaningfully with ethical issues such as bias, misinformation, and stakeholder impacts, and successfully created AI-related projects. The authors conclude that AI curricula for youth are strengthened when they combine hands-on, project-based learning with embedded ethics and accessible tools, and they offer design recommendations for future K-12 AI education in both virtual and in-person settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods curricular evaluation with descriptive pre/post analyses, thematic coding, and project assessment, but it is not an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design. The evidence is useful yet limited by small subsamples, lack of control group, and sparse standardized effect reporting.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows generally positive but mostly descriptive and non-standardized impacts on AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and engagement, with one null result on deepfake detection. Because effect sizes are largely unreported and impacts are mixed/unclear in magnitude, overall impact is best classified as yellow.

interventions.use_case: Three online AI literacy curricula for middle school students delivered through web-based activities, block-based programming tools, and guided project-based lessons to teach AI concepts and ethics.

Use of unplugged simulations, role-play, discovery activities, and game-like tasks (e.g., GANs identification, deepfake spotting, embodied feature-selection activities) to help students understand AI concepts.
In the 'How to Train Your Robot' curriculum, students used mailed low-cost Bluetooth robots and AI blocks to build machine-learning-enabled robotics projects.

finding.finding_summary: Across the three middle-school AI literacy curricula, students demonstrated improved understanding of AI concepts and applications through workshop-specific assessments and project work. In the Creative AI curriculum, correct responses improved on GAN knowledge items (e.g., one item increased from 41.2% pre to 70.6% post among n=17), and students were often able to identify generator goals (65%) and discriminator datasets (61%) in tool-based tasks, though no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Workshop-specific AI knowledge assessments, true/false GAN items, multiple-choice GAN process item, concept application tasks, project artifacts
finding.study_size: n=78 overall; Creative AI subsamples included n=11, n=17, and 58 task responses
finding.std_deviation: reported for some unrelated quiz results only; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The curricula were designed to build critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and application of AI knowledge, and student responses/projects indicate meaningful gains in these areas. In Creative AI, students identified both benefits (79 coded responses) and harms (60 coded responses) of generative AI tools and produced final AI-based creative artifacts, suggesting growth in critique, reflection, and applied design skills; however, no causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic coding of reflections and ethics responses, stakeholder/benefit-harm reasoning, final project creation and presentation
finding.study_size: n=78 overall; Creative AI ethics task included 58 student response sets; final project submissions n=33

finding.finding_summary: Students appeared highly engaged with the project-based, hands-on AI activities, and the authors report that robotics and creative tools increased excitement and participation. Evidence is primarily descriptive and qualitative rather than based on validated engagement scales, so impact is suggestive rather than precisely estimated.
finding.measure: Student reflections, observed engagement, descriptive reports of excitement and participation

finding.finding_summary: On the Creative AI deepfake-detection activity, students did not improve from pre- to post-quiz after being taught spotting strategies. Mean scores were essentially unchanged from pre-quiz M=53.44 (SD=14.73) to post-quiz M=53.55 (SD=15.18), with t(30)=-0.03, p=0.98.
finding.measure: Deepfake identification quiz scores before and after instruction
